title: Anuj Shrivatri Becomes India's 100th Grandmaster
summary:
Indian chess reached a milestone on Sunday as IM Anuj Shrivatri became the country's 100th grandmaster by winning the 7th ASEAN+ Open Chess Championship in the Philippines. The 22-year-old recovered from an opening-round defeat to finish alone in first place with 7/9.

His achievement comes 38 years after GM Viswanathan Anand earned his title to become India's first grandmaster in 1988, before going on to win five world championship titles and cement a place as India's greatest player ever.

FIDE's November list currently includes 97 Indian grandmasters, but IM Ethan Vaz, IM Rathanvel V S, in addition to Anuj, are awaiting formal confirmation of their GM titles.

India ranks fourth among federations by total grandmasters, behind Russia, the United States, and Germany. It could overtake Germany in 2027 if its recent pace of producing new GMs continues. Among active grandmasters, India already shares the lead with Russia and Germany on 74.

# | Federation | GMs | Active GMs

1 | Russia | 184 | 74

2 | United States | 115 | 73

3 | Germany | 103 | 74

4 | India | 97 | 74

5 | Ukraine | 85 | 51

6 | France | 60 | 51

7 | Spain | 60 | 45

8 | Serbia | 58 | 52

9 | China | 57 | 38

10 | Poland | 56 | 47

11 | Hungary | 53 | 37

12 | Israel | 51 | 43

13 | England | 44 | 32

14 | Netherlands | 43 | 32

15 | Armenia | 39 | 23

16 | Czech Republic | 34 | 25

17 | Bulgaria | 32 | 19

18 | Croatia | 31 | 23

19 | Georgia | 31 | 20

20 | Azerbaijan | 29 | 18

Numbers from the November 2026 FIDE rating list. Pending GM titles are excluded.

Here are some statistics about India's grandmasters:

Mean age for all GMs: 31.3. Median age for all GMs: 29.4.

Mean age for active GMs: 29.4. Median age for active GMs: 26.7.

Youngest: GM-elect Ethan Vaz (15.2 years). Oldest: GM Praveen Thipsay (67).

Eight GMs are under 20, 30 are under 25, 29 are 30 or older; 12 are 40+.

36 of the 74 were born in 2000 or later, versus 17 born before 1990.

For Anuj, the victory in the Philippines brings a rewarding end to his title chase as he entered the tournament with just one GM norm from Budapest last November, hoping to score the second one. However, the ASEAN+ championship is one of the few events where the winner is awarded a GM title directly, regardless of having enough norms or meeting the 2500 rating requirement.

"It feels very good to become a GM and that too being (India’s) 100th is also special," he told The Hindu.

"Also I feel relieved now since I was trying for GM title since last one year, and it’s really great to see hard work pay off," he added.

🇮🇳 Grandmaster #100 - @AnujShrivatri 👏 https://t.co/Fd6nISE03B

— Chess.com - India (@chesscom_in) November 9, 2026

Few people know Indian chess better than IM Sagar Shah, the co-founder of ChessBase India, who has documented the journeys of an incredible generation of rising stars, such as GMs Gukesh Dommaraju, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, Arjun Erigaisi, Nihal Sarin, and many more.

In the nearly 11 years since he launched ChessBase India with his wife, WIM Amruta Mokal, India has added around 60 grandmasters. "I think it's an amazing moment for Indian chess! I am very thrilled to see the growth and us reaching 100 GMs,” he told Chess.com.

I think it's an amazing moment for Indian chess!

—Sagar Shah

"The most amazing thing about this entire feat is that every single GM of India is alive, which just goes to show how young this achievement is," he added.

India's greatest player ever also celebrated the achievement, which coincided with Diwali.

Happy Diwali. A cracker of a 100. Congrats to @AnujShrivatri on getting India to this milestone. Funnily only today I was thinking December 2027 will be the 40th anniversary of my GM title and literally this manifested....@FIDE_chess @aicfchess

— Viswanathan Anand (@vishy64theking) November 8, 2026

For Shah, the next generation is another reason for excitement. "What I am really excited for is the next wave of talents that are coming out from Indian chess," he said.

The ChessBase India co-founder pointed to the recent 1st Chola Chess Open International Grandmasters that concluded in Chennai on Saturday, where nine players earned title norms, including seven IM norms. Among them was 10-year-old FM Sarbartho Mani, who became the sixth youngest player to ever achieve an IM norm.

10-year-old Sarbartho Mani is another Indian prodigy. Photo: Chola Chess.

Shah believes India could double its grandmaster tally within the next decade. "I think it might not be an overstatement that India could reach the 200 GMs mark by 2035," he said.

Shortly after, Shah corrected himself and said: "2035 might be a bit too long. 200 GMs in 2032!"

For Anuj, meanwhile, the milestone followed a comeback in the Philippines. He was seeded fourth in the event with 2450, behind Vietnamese IM Nguyen Quoc Hy (2474). After his opening loss, he went undefeated to score six wins and two draws.

Victories in the final two rounds secured first place, half a point ahead of GM Duc Hoa Nguyen from Vietnam. Filipino FM Alekhine Nouri finished third on tiebreak with 6/9.

Anuj's final-round win against IM James Morris from Australia clinched him the tournament and the GM title.

The title comes six years after earning the IM title as a 15-year-old in 2020. In an interview with ChessBase India that year, Anuj said he had learned chess at seven and was working mostly on his own, having previously trained with several coaches.

Speaking to The Indian Express after earning the GM title, Anuj, who had been a software engineer with a German firm, said he quit the job in order to pursue chess full time. His parents, both teachers, said they committed much of their savings to supporting his chess development.

"You need to focus at least eight to nine hours on your chess if you want to chase success in the sport. Juggling that and a software engineering job was not possible," his father, Ashok, told the newspaper.

India's newest grandmaster already has the next target set. Speaking to The Times of India, Anuj said: "I want to cross a 2600 rating, and I want to win as many tournaments as I can."

title: 3 In 4 Women Surveyed Report Discrimination Or Harassment In Chess
summary:
In a new FIDE survey, three in four women and girls who responded had experienced discrimination or harassment in chess settings, while 44% said they had considered leaving the game.

Women and girls account for roughly one in six active FIDE-registered players, with even lower representation among titled players, arbiters, trainers, and federation officials. What would help more of them take up chess, develop their potential, and stay in the game?

Those were the questions examined by FIDE’s Commission for Women’s Chess in a new survey looking at the barriers women face and how their experiences in the chess community affect their participation. The Women in Chess Representation, Participation and Development Survey was led by Arhan Boyd of the Indian School of Business and WCM Tris-Ann Richards, chair of the commission, and analyzed 672 responses from 127 federations. Its results were published on October 13.

Tris-Ann Richards is the Chair of the FIDE Commission for Women’s Chess. Photo: FIDE.

The survey was voluntary, so the findings describe respondents rather than provide a representative estimate for all women in chess. Most questions were optional, and percentages are calculated from those answering each question.

Overall, 63% of respondents reported having experienced gender bias or sexism, while 76% reported at least one of the eight forms of discrimination or harassment measured. The figures were higher among adults and titled players.

"These are the hardest numbers in the report," the authors noted.

These are the hardest numbers in the report.

—FIDE Women in Chess Survey Report

Experience | All respondents | Adults | FIDE-titled women

Gender bias/sexism | 63% | 70% | 81%

Sexual harassment/inappropriate behavior | 38% | 46% | 55%

The survey also found that 38% had experienced online abuse or harassment, while 37% reported exclusion from coaching, teams, tournaments, or leadership opportunities. Sixteen percent said they experienced gender bias or sexism often.

Image: 2026 FIDE Women in Chess Representation, Participation and Development Survey, FIDE Women in Chess Commission.

The question of keeping women in the game produced some of the report's most noteworthy findings. Among respondents aged 18–24, 64% had considered stepping away from chess. Among holders of women's FIDE playing titles, the figure was 65%.

Among respondents who reported gender bias, 56% had considered leaving chess, compared with 23% of those who had not. The association remained after accounting for factors including age, title, region, and chess involvement: respondents reporting gender bias had approximately three times the odds of having considered stepping away.

Emilia Castelao, president of the Women in Chess Foundation (WICF) welcomed FIDE's publication of the survey. The nonprofit works to create a safer, more inclusive environment for women and girls in chess.

"To be honest, it is not a surprising number to me given the amount of women that have reached out to WICF looking for support regarding harassment and discrimination and given the lack of SafePlay policy in our sport," she told Chess.com.

"I think that it most likely accurately reflects the experiences of women in chess," she added.

I think that it most likely accurately reflects the experiences of women in chess.

—Emilia Castelao, Women in Chess Foundation

Emilia Castelao is the founder and president of the Women in Chess Foundation. Photo: womeninchess.com.

Financial costs and time constraints were the most commonly selected barriers to chess development or participation. Asked to choose up to three, 66% selected costs such as travel, coaching, and entry fees, while 48% selected time pressures from school, work, or family.

Overall, 84% described the barriers they faced as major or moderate.

Image: FIDE Women in Chess Survey Report 2026.

Separate research by the Women in Chess Foundation identified similar barriers among applicants to its WICF Chessable Scholars program. Its analysis of 175 application essays found that 41% mentioned financial constraints and 33% a lack of coaching or structured training.

Participants in a group interview also described isolation, sexist comments, and stereotypes about girls' abilities. WIM Luciana Morales, director of the WICF–Chessable Scholars program, told Chess.com the two projects identified similar issues.

"Our work at the Women in Chess Foundation and FIDE’s recent report reveal strikingly similar barriers: financial constraints, unequal access to training, gender stereotypes, and the struggle to find a supportive community. Girls need investment and opportunities to develop, but they also need environments where they feel respected, supported and welcome."

Girls need investment and opportunities to develop, but they also need environments where they feel respected, supported and welcome.

—Luciana Morales

Asked what would most improve women's participation in their region, respondents to the FIDE survey most frequently selected increased financial support (65%), more local tournaments (60%), better coaching access (52%), and more women in leadership positions (46%).

The report recommends travel and entry-fee assistance, more local rated events, regional coaching programs, and clearer routes into federation leadership. It also calls for codes of conduct covering tournaments, coaching relationships, and online spaces; confidential reporting channels with independent handling; and training for arbiters and organizers to recognize and respond to harassment.

The authors concluded:

Two in three have met gender bias in chess settings, nearly two in five sexual harassment, and the women who have reached the highest levels are the ones most exposed to it. The effect on whether they stay is plain in the raw numbers and does not go away when everything else is taken into account. Chess loses a large share of its women in their early twenties, and it loses, disproportionately, the ones who have experienced bias.

The survey's authors acknowledge that their sample overrepresents active and titled players and federations that promoted the questionnaire. It also does not capture the experiences of women who have already left chess. Regional differences require care, because respondents may differ in what they recognize as discrimination and are willing to disclose.

Castelao said the findings in FIDE's survey should be followed by action from the governing chess body and its president, Timur Turlov.

"I must insist that FIDE, and Timur Turlov, finally establish an international SafePlay Policy that can be adopted by national federations in a flexible way," she said.

Tris-Ann Richards with Ulkar Umudova, member of FIDE's Commission for Women's Chess. Photo: FIDE.

In November 2023, FIDE announced a partnership with Safe Sport International to develop a safeguarding framework covering sexual harassment and the protection of children and other people at risk.

Richards, the chair of the Women's Commission, called for clear safeguarding procedures when presenting the survey at the commission's September 22 meeting in Samarkand.

"I’m very adamant on a clear policy being established to deal with such incidents, a clear FIDE policy, and that each national federation has procedures to deal with incidents like this when they occur. What I hope and will work towards is that every event, every major chess tournament, will make public what their safeguard measures are."

What I hope and will work towards is that every event, every major chess tournament, will make public what their safeguard measures are.

—Tris-Ann Richards

The findings follow years of women publicly describing harassment and its consequences. In 2023, 14 of France's leading women players drew international support when they released an open letter arguing that harassment and sexual violence contributed to women and girls leaving chess.

That same year, WIM Sabrina Chevannes, a chess coach and two-time Olympiad player for England, publicly described sexual harassment and misogyny as reasons she stopped playing professionally.

For Morales, retaining girls and women deserves as much attention as attracting them to the game.

"When even accomplished women consider leaving chess, we have to ask ourselves what we’re getting wrong. We spend so much time discussing how to bring more girls into chess. It’s time we become equally serious about giving them reasons to stay," she said.

title: FIDE President Timur Turlov visits World Senior Chess Championship
summary: FIDE President Timur Turlov visited Vrnjačka Banja, Serbia, where the World Senior Chess Championship is currently underway. Turlov met with the President of the Municipality of Vrnjačka Banja, Boban Đurović, in his office. The meeting was also attended by Andrija Jorgić, President of the Chess Federation of Serbia; Bolat Imanbayev, Ambassador of the Republic of Kazakhstan to the Republic of Serbia; and Zoran Gajić, Minister of Sports in the technical government. During the meeting, they discussed improving cooperation in the field of chess, the implementation of joint projects, and the promotion of Vrnjačka Banja as a destination for significant sporting and international gatherings.  Special attention was given to the longstanding friendship and successful cooperation between Serbia and Kazakhstan, as well as the possibilities for further strengthening these ties through future joint activities and initiatives. Following the meeting, the FIDE President visited the World Senior Chess Championship and addressed the participants before the start of Round 6. “I am pleased to welcome all participants to the FIDE World Senior Chess Championship. I would like to thank the Serbian Chess Federation and all the organisers for hosting this tournament. This year, the championship has brought together nearly 400 players from 65 countries, which clearly demonstrates the strong interest in competitions of this kind. Chess is unique in that it allows players to maintain a high level of skill and compete throughout their lives. I am confident that the experience and achievements of the participants serve as an inspiration to new generations of chess players. For FIDE, it is important that chess players of all ages have opportunities to compete in international tournaments. We are committed to further developing senior chess and supporting tournaments that bring together experienced players from around the world. I wish all participants a successful continuation of the championship, exciting games, and excellent chess,” he said. Together with Andrija Jorgić, President of the Serbian Chess Federation, Timur Turlov made the ceremonial first move in the game between Martine Dubois (MNC) and Marina Aseeva (FIDE) in the Women 65+ category. Following the opening ceremony, the FIDE President took the opportunity to personally greet some of the most distinguished figures in women’s chess, including former Women’s World Champion Nona Gaprindashvili and the legendary Swedish grandmaster Pia Cramling. After Round 6, WGM Galina Strutinskaya (FIDE) continues to dominate the Women 65+ section with a perfect 6/6, while WGM Monica Calzetta Ruiz has maintained her lead in the Women 50+ category with 5/6. In the Open 50+, GMs Kiril Georgiev and Pavel Kotsur notched up victories in Round 6 and tied for first place on 5.5/6. Meanwhile, in the Open 65+ category, eight participants share the lead on 5/6.

title: Total Chess – totally complicated
summary:
The 2025 Chess Calendar established that there are 151 official World Chess Championships. Another will be added in 2027 – the Total Chess Championship. The pilot tournament takes place in Budapest from 10 to 20 November. The field is strong, the format is complicated, and ChessBase has gone through the Total Chess webpage in an attempt to understand it. However, it is unclear whether all the rules have been correctly understood and reproduced. The following information is therefore provided without guarantee of accuracy.

Twenty-four of the world's best players will participate in the Budapest pilot, competing in Blitz, Rapid and Fast Classic, a shortened form of classical chess.

A Blitz tournament to begin (10 November)

The event begins on 10 November with a nine-round Swiss-system Blitz tournament (3+2) featuring all 24 players. But this Blitz tournament is not really that important. Or perhaps it is. Its main purpose is as a tiebreak: if players finish level on points in the group stage that follows the Blitz tournament, their placing in the Blitz tournament will decide the order. The result will also have an impact on the knockout stage that follows the Blitz tournament and the group stage.

The group stage (11 to 15 November)

In the group stage, the 24 participants are divided into four groups of six players. In each group, everyone plays everyone else twice, once with white and once with black. The games are played in "Fast Classic" mode: 45 minutes for the whole game plus 30 seconds per move. A win is worth three points, a draw one point and a loss no points. If players finish level on points, their placing in the Blitz tournament on the first day is used as the tiebreak.

The group stage determines whether a player still has a chance of winning the tournament in the knockout stage. After the group stage, the players are distributed into six separate knockout competitions according to their finishing positions: the four group winners play for the overall tournament victory and places 1 to 4. The four runners-up play for places 5 to 8, while the four sixth-placed players compete for places 21 to 24. In this way, all 24 players remain involved until the end of the tournament, but only four can fight for tournament victory after the group stage.

The Budapest tournament has a strong field | Image: Total Chess Instagram

Knockout matches (17 and 18 November)

The semifinals of the knockout competitions are scheduled for 17 and 18 November. Each knockout match consists of two mini-matches played on consecutive days. Each mini-match consists of seven games: four Blitz games (3+2), two Rapid games (15+10) and one Fast Classic game (45+30).

The games, however, are scored differently:

Discipline

Win

Draw

Loss

Blitz

1 point

0.5 points

0 points

Rapid

4 points

2 points

0 points

Fast Classic

8 points

4 points

0 points

A total of 20 points are therefore available each day. Whoever has more points after the seven games wins the mini-match. A mini-match can also end in a draw.

Vincent Keymer is also taking part | Photo: Total Chess

But things become more complicated on day two, because the score is reset to zero. In other words, whoever scores more points on a given day wins that day's match, and if one player wins both daily matches, that player advances to the final. If one of the two daily matches ends in a draw, the result of the other day decides the overall match. But if each player wins one of the two matches, or if both matches end in draws, then the winner is not decided - as one might naively assume - by who scored more points over the 14 games. Instead, the overall contest is decided by an Armageddon game. A player can therefore win the first mini-match 16-4 and lose the second 9-11. Despite having scored 25-15 overall, that player still has to play Armageddon. Perhaps not much consolation, but at least the player with the higher overall score gets to choose the colour in the Armageddon. If the overall scores are equal, however, colour choice is determined by a bidding procedure.

Final (19 and 20 November)

The winners of the semifinals play for overall victory on the final two days of the tournament, 19 and 20 November. At the same time, the remaining places are decided in the other five knockout competitions. The Total Chess world champion, however, will not be crowned until next year.

That is because the Budapest tournament is a pilot event for the Total Chess World Championship Tour, which begins in 2027. No world champion will be determined here, and no points will be awarded towards the future Tour standings either. The top three finishers will, however, earn a place in the first Tour event of 2027, provided they have not already qualified by another route. There is also a total prize fund of US$650,000, with the winner receiving $80,000.

But how exactly will the new world champion be determined?

The format of the pilot tournament may be complicated, but the regulations of the Total Chess Championship are even more complicated. Unlike the classical World Championship, the title is not decided in a single match, but through a series of tournaments followed by a final event.

At present, the Total Chess World Championship Tour consists of three tournaments, each featuring 24 players. The 24 players can qualify through various routes. These include strong results in previous Total Chess events, major FIDE tournaments, the world rankings and organiser wildcards. The participants in the three events will not necessarily be the same.

In each of the three tournaments, players receive Tour points according to their finishing positions. These points are added together. There are also bonus points for repeated tournament victories. The player with the most points after the three tournaments wins the overall Tour standings and receives the "Golden Rook" award - but that does not make him world champion. The world champion is only determined in the final event, in which the four most successful players on the Tour face one another.

But because a normal knockout competition with semifinals and a final apparently seemed too simple, the organisers came up with another twist: the two semifinal winners play for the World Championship, and this contest lasts four days and consists of two sections of two days each, known as "Races".

That means the final consists of four matches in total, each once again featuring seven games: one Fast Classic game, two Rapid games and four Blitz games. But the four matches are divided into two sets of two, and these two-match sections have been given the attractive name "Race". If one player wins both "Races", he becomes world champion. If each player wins only one "Race", however, the title is again not decided by the overall number of points scored across the four matches. Instead, two Blitz games decide the title. If there is still no winner after those Blitz games, there is another Armageddon game – and whoever wins that Armageddon game becomes the "FIDE World Combined Champion 2027".

But the "Total Chess Championship" is not only about this title. A strong performance in the "Total Chess Championship" can also help a player in the classical World Championship cycle, because FIDE has adjusted the qualification system for the 2028 Candidates accordingly. The top two players in the overall standings of the 2026–2027 Total Chess World Championship Tour will earn places in the 2028 Candidates Tournament. What matters here, however, is the Tour standings and not, as one might again naively assume, the result of the final.

In theory, the winner of the final – the "Total Chess Champion" - could fail to qualify for the Candidates Tournament because he finished "only" third in the overall Tour standings after the three tournaments, before producing a great performance in the final.

The organisers have announced that individual rules for the final event may still be adjusted based on the experience gained from the Budapest pilot tournament. Looking at the complicated regulations, however, it is difficult to know whether that is a threat or a promise.

title: Remembering Mikhail Tal
summary:
Today marks the 90th anniversary of Mikhail Tal's birth. Tal was one of the great figures in chess history, playing particularly exciting chess in his youth and becoming the youngest world champion in history in 1960. Unfortunately, he suffered from health problems throughout his life and died at a relatively young age. | Tal giving a simultaneous exhibition in 1977 (Photo: Miass City Museum Archive)

The following portrait first appeared as part of a review in Karl - Das kulturelle Schachmagazin . Reprinted here in a slightly revised version with kind permission.

An excessive chess genius - Mikhail Tal

"Misha was a genius. That is why he had this kindness. [...] But he was not a particularly easy person". That is how Angelina Tal, Mikhail Tal's widow, described her husband.

Tal was a fascinating personality. A highly gifted and intelligent artist who lived only for chess; for whom money meant nothing, who gave it away without hesitation and never owned a wallet; who was already at university at 17 because he had been able to skip two years at school; who did everything with passion and paid as little attention to his own health as he did to the other "small details" of life; who, despite serious health problems, smoked and drank excessively and was for a time addicted to morphine.

Conventions meant nothing to him. At one point he lived in a flat with his ex-wife, their son, his new girlfriend, his mother and his brother. Angelina Tal recalled that he usually got up at six in the morning and then spent (almost) the entire day on chess.

Photo source: Educhess

His games suited such a personality. Again and again, Tal produced fascinating attacks that seemed to come out of nowhere. He ventured piece sacrifices that at first glance looked "impossible", but were difficult to refute. While most players at the time painstakingly tried to avoid even the smallest weakness and clung anxiously to every pawn, Tal played with an unfamiliar dynamism and gave chess new dimensions.

Tal was born on 9 November 1936 in Riga, Latvia, to Latvian Jewish parents. When the Germans invaded Latvia on 1 July 1941, the Tal family escaped only by the narrowest of margins. They just managed to catch the last train leaving Riga, but had to leave all their belongings behind in the city.

Tal learned chess at the age of seven. He was good, but not a prodigy. In 1949, he met Alexander Koblenz, who soon became his coach and close confidant, and remained both throughout his life. Soon after that meeting, Tal's rapid rise towards the world elite began, which he reached at breathtaking speed during the 1950s. His style of play delighted chess fans around the world. The young genius loved risk, played uncompromisingly and boldly for the attack, and even against established grandmasters dared to sacrifice pieces in unclear positions.

His appearance was striking too. His penetrating gaze became legendary: it had something hypnotic about it and hinted at the passion with which Tal played. Yet despite that intimidating stare, Tal was friendly, open and approachable. Even later, when he had already become a living legend, you did not need to be a grandmaster to play, analyse and talk chess with him.

And during his rise to the world elite, Tal was not even a professional player, but was still studying. In 1958, he passed his state examination in "Russian Language and Literature" and then worked briefly as a trainee teacher before finally devoting himself entirely to chess.

It was like a fairy tale: on his very first attempt, the young Tal cleared every hurdle and qualified in 1960 as the challenger to world champion Mikhail Botvinnik, the stern patriarch of Soviet chess, whose secrets of success were hard work and discipline - in temperament, the exact opposite of Tal's artistic existence. But Tal remained true to himself and played double-edged, risky chess. His approach paid off: Tal won the World Championship match convincingly by 12½-8½.

Photo source: Russianphoto

But the miracle did not last long. Botvinnik exercised his right to a return match and prepared for it carefully. Tal seemed not to take the whole matter quite so seriously, and his trainer Koblenz despaired in his unsuccessful attempts to get Tal into the right frame of mind for the match. Tal also did something foolish for which chess lovers can now be grateful: he wrote an unusually candid book about the 1960 match in which he described his strategy, as well as his thoughts and feelings during the games. A gift to every chess lover and a fantastic book - but also ideal match preparation for Botvinnik.

Photo source: sport.ru

Tal was also in poor health during the 1961 return match. When the match was nevertheless not postponed, Tal's magic suddenly disappeared. Botvinnik's discipline, capacity for work and fanatical will to win prevailed: Tal lost 8-13 and became the youngest former world champion of all time - a title he wore with pride.

At times it may seem as though Tal never again reached his earlier heights. But that impression is misleading. Over the course of his life, he became Soviet champion no fewer than six times - something only Botvinnik also achieved - and in 1972-73, when his play had become calmer, he managed to go unbeaten for 86 consecutive games against strong opposition.

Photo: Tass

And he remained a favourite with the fans. Even though his various illnesses caused him serious problems and led to inconsistent results, he continued to produce wonderful games.

He also excelled as a chess journalist. For ten years he edited the Latvian magazine Sahs , which flourished under his leadership. His lectures and commentary on Russian television captivated even people with little knowledge of chess, and his book The Life and Games of Mikhail Tal is regarded by many as one of the best chess books of all time. In an interview with himself, Tal describes his career, his tournaments, his approach to preparation and his attitude towards chess. Tal's passion for the game is infectious, and the games themselves are a delight. Politics and his private life, however, were left out.

It is understandable that such a character had difficulties with the Soviet system. Tal was harassed by some officials and was occasionally denied permission to travel abroad. Tal probably agreed to assist Karpov as a second in his match against Korchnoi because it meant he was once again allowed to play tournaments in the West.

But Tal's excessive lifestyle eventually took its toll. He repeatedly had to undergo treatment for various illnesses and, already very ill and severely weakened, died on 28 June 1992 at the age of just 55 in a Moscow hospital following the consequences of an incorrectly performed operation. Until the end of his life, he continued to play fantastic chess. Two months before his death, at the end of April 1992, he had still taken part in a strong tournament in Barcelona and defeated Lautier in a brilliant game.

Tal sacrifices a piece in the opening in order to keep the black king in the centre and exploit his lead in development. After a series of brilliant attacking moves, a clearly favourable endgame eventually arises, which Tal wins after a number of inaccuracies by both sides.

Even in the last blitz tournament of his life, which Tal played shortly before his operation, he managed to defeat Garry Kasparov once more. Tal eventually finished third behind Kasparov and Bareev, but still ahead of Smyslov, Dolmatov and Beliavsky.

title: Pranesh wins Chola Chess Open as young talents make their mark
summary:
Pranesh M won the inaugural Chola Chess Open in Chennai, scoring 7/9 points after finishing with two consecutive victories. The Indian grandmaster ended half a point ahead of five players, including runner-up S. L. Narayanan. The tournament also saw 16-year-old Viresh Sharnarthi earn his second GM norm in ten days, while 11-year-old Sarbartho Mani secured his first IM norm. Nine title norms were achieved in total. | Photo: Devansh Singh

Pranesh finishes with two wins

GM Pranesh M emerged as the winner of the inaugural Chola Chess Open, held from 30 October to 7 November in Chennai, India. The 20-year-old grandmaster scored 7/9 points, finishing half a point ahead of a group of five players.

The tournament also produced nine title norms, with several young Indian players making notable progress towards higher titles. Among them were 16-year-old Viresh Sharnarthi, who secured his second GM norm, and 11-year-old Sarbartho Mani, who earned his first IM norm.

The nine-round classical tournament brought together 86 titled players, including 34 grandmasters and 21 international masters. With an average rating of 2412 and a minimum entry rating of 2250, the event provided a strong field in which younger competitors had opportunities to face established grandmasters. Top seed Aravindh Chithambaram (2677), second seed Pranesh (2674) and Karthikeyan Murali (2647) were the leading participants.

Pranesh was among the frontrunners throughout the competition, but his path to first place was not straightforward. Following his victory over fellow rising star Leon Luke Mendonca ( see the game with annotations below ), a defeat against S. L. Narayanan in round seven left him half a point behind the lead. Pranesh responded by defeating Harshavardhan G B in round eight, joining Narayanan, Iniyan Panneerselvam and Vitaliy Bernadskiy at the top of the standings on 6/8.

The final round saw Pranesh paired against Iniyan, with both players needing a victory to maximise their chances of taking the title. Playing white, Pranesh demonstrated excellent opening preparation. He played his first 18 moves without using any time on his clock, while his opponent had already spent a considerable amount of time considering the position.

Pranesh sacrificed the exchange to obtain the bishop pair and attacking chances. The resulting initiative proved sufficient to secure the full point, and he finished the game with more than an hour remaining on his clock.

Meanwhile, Narayanan drew with Bernadskiy, allowing Pranesh to take first place outright. Narayanan finished second on tiebreaks, ahead of Aravindh, who defeated Ethan Vaz in the final round. Ilamparthi A R and Viresh Sharnarthi also finished on 6½/9, as did Bernadskiy.

Viresh Sharnarthi earns his second GM norm

One of the tournament's most notable performances came from 16-year-old Viresh Sharnarthi, who entered the competition as the 68 th seed, with a rating of 2326. Having recently won the Western Asian Junior Championship, where he earned the IM title and his first GM norm, Viresh added a second GM norm in Chennai.

His tournament began relatively modestly, with 2½ points from his first 5 games. He then won four consecutive encounters, defeating an FM, an IM and two GMs.

The final victory was particularly important. Facing Mendonca (2629) with the black pieces, Viresh needed a win to secure his norm. He achieved exactly that, defeating the fourth seed and finishing fifth overall with 6½/9 points.

The result gave Viresh his second GM norm in the space of ten days, an unusual sequence for a player who had only recently qualified for the IM title.

Viresh Sharnarthi, who became IM and scored his maiden GM norm 10 days ago after winning the Western Asian Junior Championship, scored a win over Leon Mendonca in the final round to score his second GM Norm | Photo: Devansh Singh

Sarbartho Mani defeats two grandmasters

Another young player who attracted attention was 11-year-old Sarbartho Mani, the 71 st seed with a rating of 2311. The FIDE master began with a victory over IM Shahil Dey before defeating Greek GM Dimitris Alexakis (2536) in the second round, his first win against a grandmaster in classical chess.

Mani subsequently lost to Samvel Ter-Sahakyan and Alisher Suleymenov, but recovered with draws against two international masters. In round seven, he claimed another notable result by defeating GM Sayantan Das.

Although he scored half a point in his final two games, Mani finished with 4½/9 and a rating performance of 2451, sufficient for his first IM norm. He placed 38th in the final standings.

FM Sarbartho Mani scored his maiden IM norm | Photo: Devansh Singh
